summary: This Best Current Practice gives guidance on whether a security system needs automated key management or whether manual keying is enough. The presumption is that automated management is needed when symmetric cryptography is used, and it explains the exceptions.

eli5.summary: Keys need changing, like locks. This document helps decide when a computer should swap keys automatically and when doing it by hand is fine.

subtitle: When a protocol must use automated key management, and the narrow cases where manual keying is acceptable.

tldr.problem: Protocol designers often ask whether a security system needs automated key management or whether manually configured keys are enough.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives a presumption in favor of automated key management, a list of conditions where it MUST be used, a list of situations where manual keying may be reasonable, and rules for key size and randomness.
tldr.outcome: Anyone proposing manual keying must justify it, and that is described as a fairly high hurdle.

facts.label: Default stance
facts.value: Automated key management SHOULD be used

facts.label: Randomness target
facts.value: No better than 50% chance after searching half the key space

today: RFC 4107 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 107) published in June 2005, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Question Being Answered
sections.content:
The question often arises whether a given security system needs some form of automated key management, or whether manual keying is sufficient. The RFC says there is no single answer because circumstances differ. In general, automated key management SHOULD be used, and relying on manual key management has significant disadvantages. Occasionally it is reasonable, and the document proposes guidelines for judging that.

The guidelines are for IETF working groups and protocol authors deciding whether to mandate automated key management and whether manual key management is acceptable. The abstract adds that when symmetric cryptography is used, the presumption is that automated key management is generally but not always needed, and that a proposer of manual keying carries the burden of proof.
sections.eli5: When two computers want to keep secrets, they need keys. This RFC helps decide whether the computers should swap keys on their own or whether a person can set them up once.

sections.title: What Key Management Is
sections.content:
Key management means establishing the keying material used with a cryptographic algorithm to provide protocol security services, especially integrity, authentication and confidentiality. Automated key management derives one or more short-term session keys, and the derivation may use long-term keys to bring in authentication. How those long-term keys reach the peers, and what type they are (such as a pre-shared symmetric secret, an RSA public key or a DSA public key), is outside the document's scope. Manual key management is used to distribute them, and it can also distribute long-term session keys.

The two approaches offer very different features. An automated protocol confirms the liveness of the peer, protects against replay, authenticates the source of the short-term session key, associates protocol state with it and ensures a fresh key is generated. It can also improve interoperability by negotiating cryptographic algorithms. The RFC says these are impossible or extremely cumbersome with manual key management.

Some symmetric algorithms require implementations to prevent overuse of a given key. Automated key management can establish replacement keys before the usage limits are reached. Examples named are IPsec IKE and Kerberos, and S/MIME and TLS include automated key management functions too.
sections.eli5: Automatic key swapping is like a security guard who checks that you are really there, gives you a brand-new key each visit, and makes sure nobody replays an old one. A key you set up by hand cannot do any of that.

sections.title: When Automation Is Required
sections.content:
The RFC says key management schemes should not be designed by amateurs, and that it is almost certainly inappropriate for working groups to design their own. As evidence it recounts that the first key management protocol in the open literature was published in 1978, a flaw and a fix appeared in 1981, the fix was cracked in 1994, and a new flaw in the original was found in 1995, even though all these flaws were obvious once described. It also notes that key management software is not always large: IKEv1 can be done in less than 200 Kbytes of object code, and TLS in half that.

Automated key management MUST be used if any of these conditions hold:

  • A party will have to manage n^2 static keys, where n may become large.
  • Any stream cipher is used, such as RC4, AES-CTR or AES-CCM.
  • An initialization vector (IV) might be reused, especially an implicit IV. Random or pseudo-random explicit IVs are not a problem unless the probability of repetition is high.
  • Large amounts of data might need to be encrypted in a short time, causing frequent change of the short-term session key.
  • Long-term session keys are used by more than two parties. Multicast is a necessary exception, but multicast key management standards are emerging to avoid it.
  • The operational environment has frequent personnel or device turnover.

In general, automated key management SHOULD be used to establish session keys, and a proposal using manual key management needs strong justification in its security considerations section.
sections.eli5: Some situations are too risky for hand-made keys: too many keys to keep track of, kinds of secret codes that break if a number repeats, lots of secret traffic, or people and devices that come and go often. Then the computer must do the swapping.

sections.title: When Manual Keying May Be Reasonable
sections.content:
Manual key management may be a reasonable approach in any of these situations:

  • The environment has very limited bandwidth or very high round-trip times. Public key systems tend to need long messages and a lot of computation, and symmetric alternatives such as Kerberos often need several round trips and third parties.
  • The information being protected has low value.
  • The total traffic over the lifetime of the long-term session key will be very low.
  • The scale of each deployment is very limited.

The RFC warns that such assertions should often be viewed with skepticism. The burden of showing that manual keying is appropriate falls on its proponents, and it is a fairly high hurdle.

A system that uses manual keys needs provisions for changing them. There MUST be some way to indicate which key is in use, to avoid problems during a transition. Designs SHOULD sketch plausible ways to deploy new keys and replace old ones that might have been compromised, because a well-done mechanism can later be reused by an add-on key management scheme. Finally, lack of clarity about which parties are authenticating is not a valid reason to avoid key management. It tends to point to a deeper problem with the underlying security model.
sections.eli5: Doing it by hand can be fine when the connection is very slow, the secret is not valuable, hardly anything is sent, or there are only a few users. Even then, you must be able to tell which key is current and have a plan for swapping a stolen one.

sections.title: Key Size and Random Values
sections.content:
For public keys used to exchange symmetric keys, the RFC points to BCP 86 (RFC 3766) for key size guidance. For random number generation it points to BCP 106 (RFC 4086).

When manual key management is used, long-term shared secret values SHOULD be at least 128 bits. They MUST also be unpredictable "random" values, so that an adversary has no greater expectation than 50% of finding the value after searching half the key search space.
sections.eli5: A hand-made secret must be long and truly unguessable, like a combination picked by rolling dice rather than by choosing a birthday.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document gives guidance to working groups and protocol designers, and it says the security of the Internet is improved when automated key management is employed.

Including automated key management does not prohibit an interface for manual key management. The RFC says manual key management is very helpful for debugging, so implementations ought to provide a manual interface for that purpose, even if the protocol does not specify one.
sections.eli5: Even when keys are swapped automatically, it is handy to keep a manual setting for testing, like a spare handle to try the door by hand.
